description_full: Hydro One Limited operates as an electricity transmission and distribution company in Ontario. It operates through three segments: Transmission, Distribution, and Other. The company owns and operates approximately 30,000 circuit kilometers of high-voltage transmission lines and approximately 126,000 circuit kilometers primary low-voltage distribution lines. It provides telecommunications support services for its transmission and distribution businesses; and information and communications technology services and solutions. It serves residential, small business, commercial, and industrial customers, as well as municipal utilities. Hydro One Limited was incorporated in 2015 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

financial_summary: Hydro One Ltd is a large-cap utilities business with a $24.0B market cap on $6.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $193M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.8× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.3×.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 47% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 177% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away
Altman Z in the distress zone (1.4) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.
